posts.note: Interview with Nico Grundmann (Ember Health) on IV ketamine safety. All forward-looking claims are the interviewee's; the author's own lines are questions and present-tense remarks.
52-word podcast appearance blurb; no forward-looking statements.

Report on Helen Mayberg's talk at the BRaSSS meeting. One endorsed restatement (Brain Medicine is coming), one reported organizer plan, one reported payer concern. Mayberg's own remarks are historical.
Report on Brandon Bentzley's PCT (closed-loop SAINT continuation) talk. Trial results are past; one jocular aside about the future and one RAMHT 2026 event promotion logged.

Report on Martijn Figee's DBS talk. One third-party access forecast and one Radial-at-CTMSS commitment. Figee's clinical heuristics (TMS responders who relapse will respond to DBS) were treated as general clinical claims, not logged.

Essay on AI economics and agentic AI. Title 'AI Won't Replace Me!' is itself a negative call but is not in the post text, so it is not quoted. 'My kids will, I hope, one day read...' treated as a wish, not logged.

Q&A with Carlene MacMillan (author's wife, Radial CPO) on the Meta verdicts. Speakers are unlabeled; attribution follows the question-answer alternation. All forecasts are hers; the author calls the Radium Girls comparison 'compelling'.

statements.quote: if you calculate who’s treatment-resistant and how many infusions they’d need in a year, you’re talking about 50,000 to 60,000 medically significant adverse events annually
statements.context: Interviewee Nico Grundmann (co-founder, Ember Health) scales Ember's one-in-a-thousand rate of medically significant adverse events to the treatment-resistant subset of roughly 30 million US adults with major depression or bipolar disorder, arguing that at population scale monitored care is mandatory (seatbelt analogy).
statements.note: Quoted third party (interviewee). Conditional scale-up arithmetic, not a dated forecast.

statements.quote: Because at the population scale, it will arrive. The question is whether someone who knows how to help is there when it does.
statements.context: Closing of the interview. Grundmann says the one-in-a-thousand medically significant ketamine event is certain to occur once ketamine for depression is delivered at population scale, so a trained clinician must be in the room; he cites the FDA, APA, VA and DOD as landing on monitored IV care.
statements.note: Quoted third party. The column title frames the same thesis, but the author does not restate it in his own words.

statements.quote: Our real-world data, which we’re publishing with Mass General Brigham, shows an 84 percent treatment success rate
statements.context: Grundmann says Ember Health's real-world outcomes data (about 40,000 infusions, 2,500 patients; 84 percent treatment success, not placebo-controlled) is being published with Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School. The forward-looking element is the pending publication.
statements.note: Quoted third party; minor publication commitment.

statements.quote: Josh Brown wrote about the coming of Brain Medicine, and he’s really on to something.
statements.context: Opening of the author's report from the Brain Stimulation as a Subspecialty Symposium (BRaSSS). The author endorses Josh Brown's forecast that 'Brain Medicine' is coming as a discipline, linking it to Nolan Williams and Shan Siddiqi's push for a new intersectional specialty; he adds that Helen Mayberg is a giant in 'the field that isn’t even officially a field yet'.
statements.note: Endorsed restatement of Josh Brown's forecast; the author says he has written this before.

statements.quote: The basic project is ambitious: take a field that currently trains people through apprenticeships, disease-specific fellowships, and self-teaching, and build a real accreditation pathway. The fellowship would cover TMS, DBS, ECT, VNS, eCOT-AS, eTNS, PRISM, and other modalities, and it would be open to psychiatrists, neurologists, and neurosurgeons alike.
statements.context: The author describes the BRaSSS organizers' plan to turn brain stimulation into a formally recognized, accredited clinical subspecialty with a multi-modality fellowship. He reports they have voted on the name, launched a nonprofit to run accreditation, are certifying existing programs, and include a grandparenting provision.
statements.note: Reported plan of the meeting organizers; the author is sympathetic ('proud to be in the room') but does not forecast success.

statements.quote: There is a concern that insurers will use board certification as an excuse to restrict reimbursement.
statements.context: Reported worry at the BRaSSS meeting about a side effect of creating a brain stimulation board certification: payers could limit reimbursement for TMS, DBS, ECT and similar treatments to board-certified clinicians.
statements.confidence_phrase: There is a concern that ... will
statements.note: Reported concern of unnamed meeting participants; the author neither adopts nor rejects it.

statements.quote: Yours truly, furiously taking notes on the future anyway!
statements.context: Bracketed aside right after Brandon Bentzley (Magnus Medical, Salma Health) stresses that the personalized continuation protocol (wearable monitoring plus rescue days of SAINT) is experimental and carries no FDA label. The author signals he regards closed-loop SAINT continuation as the future of treatment-resistant depression care.
statements.note: Borderline: jocular aside with an implicit expectation and no specific claim.

statements.quote: You can see Salma, Radial, Definium, NRx, Beckley Clinical, Ampa, SimplePractice, GrayMatters Health, MDhub, Psyrin, and more teams speak live and in person on the first night of the APA annual meeting at RAMHT 2026 SF—May Edition!
statements.context: Closing promotion. The author's own event, RAMHT 2026 San Francisco (May edition), is scheduled for the first night of the APA annual meeting, with the listed companies speaking.
statements.horizon_text: on the first night of the APA annual meeting at RAMHT 2026 SF—May Edition
statements.note: Author's own organization (RAMHT, Radial, Ampa, Psyrin); event and speaker lineup commitment.

statements.quote: But I think we’re nearing a point where DBS is becoming more precise, and as soon as it’s there, it’s going to be much easier for all of you to program. You’re just going to have to look at the patient and their symptom-specific or brain-symptom-specific profile. And then it’s defined: the right dose, the right target. You don’t have to endlessly cycle through different settings. And that’s going to meaningfully improve access.
statements.context: Martijn Figee (Mount Sinai, Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics) answering an audience question on how to scale DBS for psychiatry: individualized tractography-based targeting will soon make programming simple enough for general psychiatrists and will improve access.
statements.horizon_text: nearing a point ... as soon as it’s there
statements.note: Quoted third party (talk transcript); the author reports approvingly but does not restate the forecast.

statements.quote: The collaboration has already yielded one accepted publication, but you will have to join Radial at CTMSS to read more.
statements.context: Closing note. The Radial and Mount Sinai (Figee, Kopell) DBS collaboration has an accepted publication; the author says Radial will present it at the CTMSS meeting, where a Radial poster was accepted.
statements.note: Author's own organization (Radial); conference presentation commitment.

statements.quote: It is now pretty clear to me that AI is going to be a huge technology. Chatbots are good, but agents? Holy cow.
statements.context: After arguing that AI companies have thin margins and subsidize users, the author reports that Claude Code fixed the image files for his book Inessential Pharmacology, and concludes that AI, especially agentic AI, will be a huge technology.
statements.confidence_phrase: pretty clear to me that ... is going to be
statements.note: Post title is 'AI Won’t Replace Me!'. The essay's economics section calls AI profitability an open question before this reversal.

statements.quote: AI will absolutely replace a lot of things I do every day, but I would rather not be doing. It is already doing so. That will, predictably, change me.
statements.context: The author predicts AI will take over many of his own daily tasks (the tedious ones) and that this will change him, in tension with the post title 'AI Won’t Replace Me!'.
statements.note: Compound: task replacement plus personal change.

statements.quote: And it will change you, and it will change our kids. It will replace us with our future selves, who will have to think hard to imagine how it used to be.
statements.context: Continuation of the AI essay; the author extends the prediction to readers and to his 9-year-old twins: AI will change everyone so much that the pre-AI way of working will be hard to imagine.
statements.note: Broad societal claim with no date.

statements.quote: Savor this moment, the end of an era—it will never be so hard to do boring things ever again.
statements.context: The author declares the present the end of an era: because of agentic AI, tedious tasks will never again be as hard as they are now.

statements.quote: I feel like there’s a more apt comparison for how this might play out, and that’s the Radium Girls from the 1920s and 1930s.
statements.context: Carlene MacMillan (author's wife, Chief Product Officer at Radial, AACAP committee co-chair) on the Meta lawsuit verdicts in California and New Mexico: she expects the social media liability story to play out like the Radium Girls litigation, which produced workplace safety regulation (OSHA), rather than like tobacco.
statements.note: Quoted third party (Q&A with Carlene MacMillan); the author later calls it 'a compelling comparison'.

statements.quote: As long as these things are free with no consequence, I don’t see how this gets solved, even with age-gating.
statements.context: MacMillan argues social media harm to children will not be solved while the platforms are free, even with age-gating; she then proposes a pay-after-a-free-hour pricing model as a check.
statements.horizon_text: As long as these things are free
statements.note: Quoted third party; negative conditional forecast.

statements.quote: These verdicts, even though the dollar amounts are small, signal a shift in perception. The liability is becoming real. And what I hope follows, what has to follow, the way OSHA followed the Radium Girls, is actual regulation. Not just fines that get treated as a cost of doing business, but enforceable product standards.
statements.context: MacMillan answering the author's 'where does this go from here?': the California product-defect verdict (about $6 million) and the New Mexico encrypted-chat case mark platform liability becoming real, and she expects and demands enforceable product standards (for example a ban on infinite scroll).
statements.confidence_phrase: is becoming real ... I hope ... has to follow
statements.note: Compound: trend claim (liability becoming real) plus a hope/must clause about regulation; quoted third party.

statements.quote: I think they’ll give us the regulatory framework we should have built at the start.
statements.context: MacMillan answering the author's question 'The Radium Girls gave us OSHA. What do you think the social media plaintiffs might give us?': she predicts the Meta plaintiffs will produce a regulatory framework for social media.
statements.note: Quoted third party; the author's question frames the analogy as 'compelling'.

statements.quote: And just like then, it’s going to take the visible suffering of vulnerable young women, working hard, wanting to be something, being preyed upon, before we finally say this is not okay. We regulate everything else. We can regulate this.
statements.context: MacMillan continues: as in the 1910s and 1920s manufacturing era, regulation of social media will come only after visible harm to vulnerable young women; she asserts it can be regulated.
statements.confidence_phrase: it’s going to take ... before we finally
